correctness.rationale: The source join formula has \(\mu(\alpha,\beta)>1\) because its radical exceeds \(\alpha+\beta\) by the strict squared difference \(4\alpha\beta\). The exact \(s\)-composable sum-product identity then forces at least one factor \(h_i-1<1\), hence one step \(h_i<2\). The long-step and overshoot mass bounds are direct decompositions of \(H_N=\sum_i h_i=U_N-1\). Substitution of the exact phase law and its positive phase minimum gives the uniform \(O(N^{1-p})\) deficit. The maximum-step bound is the exact averaging inequality.

source_inspections.title: Accelerated Gradient Descent via Long Steps
source_inspections.trigger: Closest earlier primary literature explicitly interpreting steps above 2 as the mechanism for accelerated plain gradient descent.

value.rationale: The recent paper makes the role of carefully organized long steps central but its phase theorem is stated at the level of the terminal rate scalar. The new statement converts that scalar law into a concrete structural description of the actual step schedule: a short step below the classical boundary is unavoidable, the largest step must diverge, and asymptotically essentially all cumulative stepsize mass is contributed by the long-step excess. This directly clarifies how recursive no-momentum acceleration allocates its step budget and distinguishes the mechanism from simply taking every step above the one-step stability boundary.
